parameters.name: exception_id

parameters.name: resolution
parameters.notes: The correction that resolves it (BR-4). Each of the four exception kinds needs a different one: an asset **moved** is a reassignment, one **broken** is a maintenance record, one **missing** or **quietly disposed of** is a disposal — and a disposal recorded as lost is a write-off and probably an investigation (BR-3, UC-18-11 BR-11).

parameters.name: resolution_reason
parameters.notes: 10 to 500 characters, the resolver's own. Required (BR-4, E4) — it is the record of why the register was changed to disagree with what it said before.

fields.name: resolution
fields.description: The correction proposed.

fields.description: What approving it will actually do — end an assignment and begin another, add a maintenance record and move the condition, or retire the asset from the register.

fields.description: What the register says the asset is worth. Where the resolution is a disposal for a missing asset, this is what is being written off (UC-18-11 BR-5).

fields.name: goes_through_disposal_approval
fields.description: Where the resolution is a disposal, it carries the disposal's own approval and its own thresholds on top of this one (UC-18-11 BR-2).

fields.name: approver
fields.description: The School Admin. Never the verifier who raised it (BR-4, E5).

errors.meaning: A correction was proposed with no reason.

planningRules.rule: Match the correction to the kind of exception, and never guess it. An asset moved needs a reassignment, one broken needs a maintenance record, one missing needs a disposal — and calling a missing asset "moved" is how a loss becomes a paperwork exercise (BR-3, BR-4).

Never write the reason. It is the record of why the register was changed to say something different from what it said before, and it is read long after everybody has forgotten the walk round (BR-4, E4).

Say what approving will actually do. A disposal here retires the asset and writes off its value, and it carries the disposal use case's own approval on top of this one — resolving an exception is not a bookkeeping tidy-up (BR-4, BR-7).
Say that nothing has changed yet. The register moves on the approval and never on the proposal (BR-7, E7).
Say what a missing asset is worth, and that nothing further follows. Beyond a disposal recorded as lost there is no process at all for an asset that is never found (OQ-3, OQ-4).

planningRules.rule: Say what the correction actually did. "Resolved" covers a reassignment, a repair record and a write-off, and only one of those means the school has lost something (BR-3, BR-4).

Never approve a correction the acting user proposed. One person walking round, deciding what was wrong and changing the register to match is the arrangement the separation exists to prevent (BR-4, E5).

Say how many exceptions are still outstanding. The verification does not complete until every one is resolved, and a partially-resolved verification leaves the register drifting exactly where it was found to be wrong (BR-4, E6).

Where the correction is a disposal, say it is raised rather than done. It carries its own approval and its own thresholds, and that use case cannot complete while nothing in the system calculates a book value (BR-4, BR-7).
branch_id comes from $session.

reversal.statement: A resolved exception is terminal, and neither the verification nor the exception is ever deleted (BR-9, E9). A correction found to be wrong is undone through whatever route its own use case provides — another reassignment, a further maintenance record — not by reversing this.

The disposal has its own approval, its own value threshold, and it is recorded as lost — a write-off of PKR 68,000 which the specification itself calls probably an investigation. Say plainly that the disposal cannot be completed at all as the system stands: nothing calculates depreciation, so the asset carries no remaining book value and the gain or loss cannot be computed.

fields.description: Scope, date, who verified, assets checked, assets unchecked and exceptions raised.

fields.name: days_since_last
fields.description: How long since anybody walked round. A register unchecked since June is a list rather than a record (BR-5, E10).

fields.description: Assets no verification has ever covered. Their presence has never been confirmed by anybody (BR-5).

fields.name: exceptions_by_kind
fields.description: Missing, moved, borrowed and not returned, or broken and quietly disposed of. Only one of the four means the school has lost something (BR-3).

fields.name: unresolved
fields.description: Exceptions with no approved correction. Every one holds its verification open, and the register is known to be wrong and still in use (BR-4, E6).

fields.name: repeat_exceptions
fields.description: Assets that were exceptions at more than one verification, and custodians who appear at more than one. An asset missing at every verification is not an accident (BR-8).

fields.name: total_value_missing
fields.description: What the register says the assets recorded as missing were worth. Nothing escalates on value — every missing asset is treated the same (OQ-4).

fields.name: scopes_never_checked
fields.description: Rooms, people or departments no verification has ever covered. Where a scope is a room, note that nothing in the system creates a room register at all (BR-10, OQ-5).

errors.meaning: The acting user cannot see the verification screens.
errors.note: The use case writes no exception for it.

planningRules.rule: Lead with how long it has been. Every claim the register makes rests on somebody having walked round, and "nothing since June" answers most questions about whether it can be relied on (BR-5, E10).
Name the unresolved exceptions. For each of those the school knows its register is wrong and is still using it, and the verification that found the problem never completed (BR-4, E6).
Name the assets and the custodians that come up more than once. An asset missing at every verification is not an accident, and neither is a custodian who appears in three (BR-8).
Give the value of what is recorded as missing, and say that nothing escalates on it. Every missing asset is treated the same whatever it was worth (OQ-4).
Name what has never been checked at all — assets and scopes both. Never verified and verified clean read identically on the register (BR-5, BR-6).

reversal.statement: A read changes nothing. The record it reads is never deleted (BR-9, E9).
